abstract.p: Arterial thrombosis remains a leading cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality despite widespread use of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin and P2Y12 inhibitors. Although these agents reduce ischemic events, their efficacy is counterbalanced by dose-dependent bleeding and their inability to distinguish pathological platelet activation from physiological hemostasis. Recent advances in platelet biology have shifted therapeutic development toward hemostasis-sparing antiplatelet strategies—approaches designed to selectively inhibit thrombosis while preserving baseline hemostatic function. These strategies target upstream adhesion receptors (GPVI, GPIb–vWF, CLEC-2) and receptor-proximal intracellular signaling nodes (SYK, BTK, PI3Kβ, PLCγ2, NADPH oxidases) that are preferentially engaged under high-shear or strongly prothrombotic conditions. Early-phase clinical and translational studies of such agents demonstrate antithrombotic efficacy with minimal impact on bleeding time, supporting their mechanistic selectivity. In parallel, contemporary clinical practice increasingly utilizes individualized risk assessment, platelet function testing, and genetic profiling to tailor treatment intensity. This integration of mechanism-selective agents with patient-specific risk evaluation forms the basis of precision-based thrombosis prevention, a framework aimed at aligning the duration and depth of platelet inhibition with the dynamic balance between ischemic and bleeding risk. Together, these developments mark a paradigm shift from broad platelet suppression toward rational, context-adaptive, and safer antiplatelet therapy.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Arterial thrombosis remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. According to the World Health Organization, 19.8 million people died from cardiovascular disease (CVD) in 2022, accounting for approximately 32% of all global deaths, with nearly 85% attributable to myocardial infarction and stroke—canonical atherothrombotic events driven by platelet-rich arterial thrombosis. This burden is unevenly distributed, with more than three-quarters of CVD deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries, underscoring an urgent need for safer and more deployable antithrombotic strategies worldwide (World Health Organization, 2025). In the United States alone, the American Heart Association reports persistently high mortality and economic costs, emphasizing that prevention of arterial thrombosis, most notably in acute coronary syndrome (ACS), remains pivotal to improving cardiovascular outcomes (Martin et al., 2024).

Current clinical management relies primarily on dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT), combining aspirin and a purinergic ADP receptor (P2Y12) inhibitor, as the cornerstone of secondary prevention following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or ACS (Bhatt et al., 2006). Although DAPT has substantially reduced recurrent ischemic events, its clinical utility is constrained by the inevitable trade-off between antithrombotic efficacy and bleeding liability (Capodanno and Greco, 2023). Bleeding complications are associated with increased mortality and often necessitate early therapy discontinuation, undermining the net clinical benefit—particularly in high-bleeding-risk (HBR) populations such as the elderly, those with renal impairment, or patients with prior hemorrhagic events. In parallel, inter-individual variability in platelet response, especially in carriers of cytochrome P450 2C19 (CYP2C19) loss-of-function alleles treated with clopidogrel, contributes to residual thrombotic risk despite guideline-directed therapy.

Over the past decade, clinical strategy has evolved from the conventional “more is better” paradigm toward a precision-oriented, risk-adapted approach. Numerous randomized trials, including TWILIGHT, GLOBAL LEADERS, STOPDAPT-2, have demonstrated that abbreviated or de-escalated DAPT regimens can reduce bleeding without increasing ischemic events, supporting a transition toward individualized antiplatelet therapy guided by dynamic assessment of thrombotic and bleeding risks (Hong et al., 2021; Mehran et al., 2019; Watanabe et al., 2019). Yet, even within optimized regimens, a considerable proportion of patients continue to experience ischemic complications, highlighting those current antiplatelet drugs—targeting broad amplification pathways such as cyclooxygenase (COX)-1-mediated thromboxane A₂ (TXA2) or adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-dependent P2Y12 signaling—do not discriminate between pathologic thrombosis and physiologic hemostasis.

Recent mechanistic and translational discoveries have therefore catalyzed a paradigm shift in antiplatelet drug development (Gawaz et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2025). The emerging objective is hemostasis-sparing antiplatelet therapy—that is, the selective inhibition of pathologic platelet activation and thrombus formation while preserving baseline hemostatic function. This concept centers on two interrelated mechanistic axes:

(i) platelet surface receptors such as P2Y12, glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (GPIIb/IIIa), glycoprotein VI (GPVI), Glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex (GPIb-IX-V)–von Willebrand factor (vWF), C-type lectin-like receptor 2 (CLEC-2), which mediate initial platelet tethering and activation on damaged or inflamed endothelium; and

(ii) intracellular signaling kinases and enzymatic cascades such as spleen tyrosine kinase (SYK), Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK), phosphoinositide 3-kinase β (PI3Kβ), phospholipase Cγ2 (PLCγ2), 12-lipoxygenase (12-LOX), protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) that propagate activation, granule secretion, integrin αIIbβ3 activation, and procoagulant conversion.

sec.title: Adhesion under arterial shear
sec.p: Arterial thrombosis unfolds on a damaged or inflamed arterial wall under high shear. The initiating step is tethering/adhesion of circulating platelets to exposed collagen/vWF, followed by activation and aggregation into a platelet-rich thrombus (Rana et al., 2019). First, GPIb–IX–V on platelets catches multimeric vWF strings exposed on subendothelium; this shear-dependent bond allows rolling and translocation across the surface and positions platelets over collagen-rich niches. Second, GPVI, an Ig-superfamily receptor that constitutively associates with Fc receptor γ-chain (FcRγ), binds fibrillar collagen. These encounters provide the spatial and mechanical context in which signaling begins and define the arterial (high-shear) selectivity of ensuing thrombus formation (Bye et al., 2016; Li et al., 2010) (Fig. 1).

sec.title: ITAM signaling and Ca2+ mobilization
sec.p: Collagen engagement is mediated predominantly by GPVI, a member of the immunoglobulin superfamily that constitutively associates with the FcRγ. Collagen binding clusters GPVI–FcRγ complexes and triggers immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM) phosphorylation, recruitment/activation of SYK, and propagation to PLCγ2. PLCγ2 hydrolyzes phosphatidylinositol 4,5-biphosphate (PIP₂), generating inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate (IP₃) and diacylglycerol (DAG) to drive Ca²⁺ release, granule secretion, and inside-out activation of integrin αIIbβ3—the final common aggregator by stabilizing platelet-platelet cohesion. Multiple canonical studies and reviews have mapped this pathway and its crosstalk with Src-family kinases and G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling (Estevez and Du, 2017).

sec.title: Amplification loops
sec.p: Activated platelets amplify the response via secretion of ADP and synthesis of TXA₂, which stimulate P2Y12 (Gi-coupled) and thromboxane-prostanoid (TP) receptors, respectively, reinforcing integrin activation and thrombus growth. Thrombin generated on the platelet surface further augments platelet activation via protease-activated receptor 1/4 (PAR1/PAR4). These amplification loops are the historical targets of aspirin (COX-1) and P2Y12 antagonists (Bye et al., 2016) (Fig. 1).

sec.title: Thrombo-inflammation and leukocyte crosstalk
sec.p: Beyond hemostasis, platelets orchestrate thrombo-inflammatory circuits: they bind leukocytes by expressing P-selectin that ligates P-selectin glycoprotein ligand-1 (PSGL-1) on leukocytes (Kling et al., 2013), stabilize inflamed microvasculature and foster Neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation (Colicchia et al., 2023). NETs interlace with vWF and fibrin, stiffen clots, and propagate microvascular occlusion. These processes couple immunity and thrombosis (immunothrombosis), amplifying injury in ACS, stroke, infection, and ischemic/reperfusion settings. These axes extend therapeutic reach beyond classical agonists to adhesion receptors (GPVI, GPIb), hemITAM CLEC-2 (via podoplanin in inflamed/tumor endothelium), and signaling nodes (SYK/BTK/PI3Kβ) as hemostasis-sparing opportunities because they are preferentially engaged under high shear or strong stimulus (Mack et al., 2024; Muller et al., 2015).

sec.title: CURRENT ANTIPLATELET AGENTS AND LIMITATIONS
sec.p: Current antiplatelet regimens predominantly target amplification and effector pathways. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1, blocking TXA₂ production, and thus reduces platelet aggregation through the TXA₂ axis. P2Y12 receptor inhibitors (clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor) suppress ADP-mediated platelet activation and reinforce the antithrombotic effect of aspirin. In certain high-risk settings, GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors, which block final common fibrinogen binding, and PAR1 antagonists have also been utilized (Jourdi et al., 2021).

sec.title: Mechanisms of current agents
sec.p: Aspirin (COX-1 inhibitor): Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) remains the cornerstone of antiplatelet therapy and the most widely prescribed drug in cardiovascular medicine. It acts through irreversible acetylation of the serine 530 residue in platelet COX-1, thereby blocking the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H₂, the precursor of TXA₂ (Cyrus et al., 2002). By preventing TXA₂ generation, aspirin reduces platelet recruitment and aggregation at sites of vascular injury, curtailing the self-amplifying wave of activation that drives arterial thrombosis. Low-dose regimens (75-100 mg daily) selectively suppress platelet COX-1 while minimizing inhibition of endothelial COX-2–derived prostacyclin, which exerts vasodilatory and antithrombotic effects (Cyrus et al., 2002; Jiang et al., 2020; Xian et al., 2015). Large-scale randomized trials established aspirin as the foundation of secondary prevention in myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and peripheral artery disease, reducing serious vascular events by ≈25% (Frelinger et al., 2006). It is equally indispensable in combination with P2Y₁₂ inhibitors after PCI (which is called DAPT). Its strengths include once-daily dosing, low cost, and proven reduction of MI/stroke in secondary prevention. Limitations are dose-independent GI and intracranial bleeding, and non-selective suppression of thromboxane signaling that does not discriminate pathological from physiological activation (Hirsch, 2021; Hopkins, 2012).

P2Y12 inhibitors (clopidogrel → prasugrel, ticagrelor): The platelet P2Y₁₂ receptor is a Gᵢ-coupled purinergic receptor that responds to ADP released from dense granules of activated platelets (Dorsam and Kunapuli, 2004). ADP binding suppresses adenylate cyclase (AC), decreases cyclic AMP (cAMP), and stabilizes integrin αIIbβ3 activation, thereby amplifying and sustaining platelet aggregation (André et al., 2003; Li et al., 2023). Pharmacologic antagonism of P2Y₁₂ prevents this positive-feedback loop and represents the key synergistic partner to aspirin in DAPT. Clopidogrel (Savi et al., 1998), prasugrel (Jakubowski et al., 2007), and ticagrelor (Husted and Van Giezen, 2009) underpin DAPT after PCI/ACS (Bhatt et al., 2006; Jacob et al., 2012; Mehran et al., 2019). Clopidogrel requires CYP-dependent bioactivation creating inter-individual variability such as CYP2C19 loss-of-function (Mega et al., 2009), whereas prasugrel and ticagrelor provide more potent and consistent inhibition with superior ischemic protection in ACS subsets but at the expense of higher bleeding in vulnerable cohorts-fueling strategies that de-escalate potency or shorten DAPT once peak thrombotic risk abates (Yanachkov et al., 2016). Genetic polymorphisms, including CYP2C19 loss-of-function, and drug–drug interactions remain practical concerns that support individualized selection and, in some strategies, de-escalation after the early risk window. These limitations have stimulated interest in next-generation P2Y₁₂ inhibitors that retain rapid onset and robust platelet inhibition while enabling greater dosing flexibility and potentially preserving physiological hemostasis. Selatogrel, a highly selective and reversible P2Y₁₂ antagonist administered subcutaneously, is currently being evaluated in the phase III SOS-AMI trial for early, out-of-hospital treatment of suspected myocardial infarction (Zalzal et al., 2025). Selatogrel produces potent inhibition within 15-30 min and allows near-complete recovery of platelet function within ~24 h after a single dose. Preclinical arterial injury models demonstrated that selatogrel achieves strong antithrombotic effects while preserving mural platelet aggregates that support vascular sealing, suggesting a potentially wider therapeutic window compared with oral thienopyridines. In phase II studies in chronic coronary syndrome and acute myocardial infarction, selatogrel was associated only with trivial, non-serious bleeding events (e.g., injection-site bruising or minor access-site oozing) and no treatment-related major bleeding. However, these trials were not powered to detect differences in bleeding outcomes, and no human study to date has shown a definitive reduction in major bleeding relative to conventional long-acting P2Y₁₂ inhibitors. Thus, while the pharmacokinetic reversibility and self-administration potential of selatogrel position it as a promising context-adaptive, bleeding-aware antiplatelet option, its true hemostasis-sparing capacity awaits confirmation in adequately powered outcome trials. Other reversible or short-acting agents—such as R-138727 (Algaier et al., 2008) and nanoparticle-based delivery platforms—are in earlier developmental stages and similarly aim to balance ischemic efficacy with improved safety.

PAR-1 antagonism (vorapaxar) and thrombin pathways: Thrombin-mediated platelet activation represents one of the most potent amplifiers of arterial thrombosis. Thrombin exerts its effects through PARs, primarily PAR1 and PAR4, which are expressed on the platelet surface (Brito and Tricoci, 2013). Upon proteolytic cleavage by thrombin, the N-terminal ectodomain of these receptors exposes a tethered ligand that binds intramolecularly to activate intracellular signaling cascades. This self-activation mechanism triggers G-protein–coupled signaling pathways, leading to Ca²⁺ mobilization, granule secretion, and integrin αIIbβ3 activation, thereby reinforcing platelet aggregation and thrombus stability (Negrescu et al., 1995). Although both receptors contribute to thrombin signaling, they display distinct activation thresholds and kinetic profiles that define their physiological functions.

PAR1 is a high-affinity, rapidly activated receptor that responds to low nanomolar thrombin concentrations and mediates the early, essential phase of hemostatic platelet activation. In contrast, PAR4 has lower thrombin affinity and exhibits slower but more sustained Ca²⁺ signaling, driving dense-granule release, cytoskeletal contraction, thrombus consolidation, and fibrin-rich clot maturation—processes that disproportionately contribute to pathological thrombus propagation, particularly under high-shear arterial flow (Liu et al., 2021). This division of labor implies that inhibiting PAR1 disrupts primary hemostasis, whereas selectively modulating PAR4 may primarily blunt the amplification and stabilization phases of thrombosis.

Among pharmacologic modulators of this pathway, vorapaxar is the first and only PAR1 antagonist approved for clinical use (Tricoci et al., 2012). It is indicated in the United States for patients with a history of myocardial infarction (MI) or peripheral artery disease (PAD), where it acts as an irreversible inhibitor of PAR1, blocking thrombin-mediated platelet activation (Cavender et al., 2015; Morrow et al., 2013; Tricoci et al., 2012). Vorapaxar has a rapid onset (1-2 h) but a prolonged half-life (effective ~3-4 days, terminal ~8 days), resulting in sustained platelet inhibition even after drug discontinuation. The efficacy of vorapaxar has been evaluated in large randomized controlled trials, including TRACER and TRA 2°P–TIMI 50, which enrolled patients with prior MI, stroke, and/or PAD. When added to standard antiplatelet therapy—either single (SAPT) or dual (DAPT)—vorapaxar reduced composite ischemic endpoints such as cardiovascular death, MI, and stroke compared with standard therapy alone. However, these gains were offset by a substantial increase in moderate and severe bleeding, particularly intracranial hemorrhage in patients with prior stroke or advanced age and low body weight (Morrow et al., 2013). Consequently, such populations were excluded from the FDA-approved indication. Overall, vorapaxar demonstrates that targeting PAR1 can provide incremental ischemic benefit, but its narrow therapeutic window and irreversible inhibition limit broader applicability.

These limitations have shifted therapeutic development toward reversible and PAR4-selective antagonists that preserve the early PAR1-dependent hemostatic response while attenuating the PAR4-mediated propagation phase of thrombosis. Small-molecule PAR4 antagonists such as BMS-986120 demonstrate potent and selective inhibition of PAR4-driven platelet activation, markedly reducing arterial thrombus formation in preclinical models without significantly prolonging bleeding time (Merali et al., 2022; Rwibasira Rudinga et al., 2018; Wilson et al., 2018). Mechanistically, PAR4 blockade suppresses sustained Ca²⁺ signaling, granule secretion, and clot stabilization while maintaining the initial platelet plug formation required for vascular sealing. This mechanistic selectivity supports the concept that PAR4 antagonism may achieve true hemostasis-sparing antithrombotic activity, directly addressing the safety limitations that hindered PAR1-directed therapy. Ongoing research is thus directed toward developing reversible or PAR4-selective antagonists, which may attenuate thrombin-driven platelet activation while minimizing bleeding liability.

sec.title: Limitations of current strategies
sec.p: (1) Bleeding liability: The major adverse effect of all current antiplatelet agents is bleeding, which may lead to morbidity, transfusion, or therapy discontinuation (Park, 2022). Current agents broadly inhibit platelet activation, affecting both pathologic and physiologic responses. This indiscriminate suppression is the root of bleeding complications. In many trials, the net clinical benefit is weighed carefully against bleeding risk, especially in elderly or comorbid populations. (2) Residual thrombotic risk: Even under optimal DAPT (Hara et al., 2021), a significant proportion of patients experience ischemic events, suggesting incomplete control of upstream adhesion/signaling or non-platelet thrombotic drivers. Many antiplatelet agents primarily target amplification and effector steps, including TXA₂ generation, ADP-mediated signaling, and integrin binding. Upstream adhesion events, receptor clustering, signal initiation, or conversion to procoagulant platelets are less well addressed by current therapy. (3) Inter-individual variability (genetics, pharmacokinetics, comorbidity) yields high residual platelet reactivity in a meaningful subset. (4) Therapeutic strategies are often static, while patient risk evolves over time—fueling interest in shortened DAPT/monotherapy approaches.

sec.title: Evidence for de-escalation and abbreviated DAPT
sec.p: Contemporary randomized trials demonstrate that risk-adapted approaches can lower bleeding without excess ischemia in PCI populations. In TWILIGHT, high-risk patients on 3-month DAPT who continued ticagrelor alone had significantly less BARC 2-5 bleeding vs. continued DAPT, with noninferior ischemic outcomes (Mehran et al., 2019). Additional data-notably studies evaluating early aspirin discontinuation with ticagrelor monotherapy-similarly support shorter DAPT horizons in selected cohorts (Hong et al., 2024; Tarantini et al., 2025); newer updates continue to report noninferiority or superiority for bleeding while maintaining ischemic protection, although generalizability across all risk states remains an area of active research.

sec.title: Rationale for next-generation (“hemostasis-sparing”) targets
sec.p: Given these gaps, there is a compelling rationale to explore targeted inhibition of surface receptors and intracellular kinase pathways that lie upstream of broad platelet activation. By intervening at these nodal points, one may attenuate pathological thrombosis while potentially preserving basal platelet function under low-stimulus conditions.

Because legacy drugs broadly suppress amplification pathways (TXA₂/ADP) or final aggregation, they inevitably attenuate physiologic hemostasis. Upstream interventions—adhesion receptors (GPVI, GPIb–vWF, CLEC-2) and signal-initiation/propagation nodes (SYK, BTK, PI3Kβ, PLCγ2)—promise context-dependent selectivity and therefore a lower bleeding penalty.

sec.title: EMERGING TARGETS IN ANTIPLATELET THERAPY
sec.p: Key molecular targets and their corresponding novel antiplatelet agents are illustrated in Fig. 2 and summarized in Table 1.

sec.title: Surface receptor & Adhesion receptor
sec.p: Glycoprotein VI (GPVI): GPVI is the principal platelet collagen receptor that initiates platelet adhesion and activation following vascular injury. Upon collagen engagement, GPVI forms a complex with the FcRγ chain, leading to ITAM phosphorylation and downstream activation of SYK and PLCγ2, culminating in Ca²⁺ mobilization, granule secretion, and integrin αIIbβ3 activation (Massberg et al., 2003; Nieswandt and Watson, 2003). Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of GPVI reduces arterial thrombosis in animal models while largely sparing physiological bleeding time (Lockyer et al., 2006). Revacept, a soluble dimeric GPVI-Fc fusion protein that blocks platelet–collagen interaction, has been evaluated in clinical trials (Ungerer et al., 2011). The ISAR-PLASTER study (NCT01946854) and phase II REVACEPT–Carotid trial demonstrated safety and a reduction in microembolic signals without an increase in bleeding (Mayer et al., 2021). More recently, glenzocimab (ACT017), a humanized Fab targeting GPVI, showed favorable pharmacokinetics and safety in phase II trials in stroke and myocardial infarction patients (Mazighi et al., 2024; Renaud et al., 2020; Wichaiyo et al., 2022). These data collectively support GPVI as a promising hemostasis-sparing target for arterial thrombosis.

GPIb–vWF axis: The GPIb–IX–V complex mediates platelet tethering to vWF under high-shear conditions, such as in stenotic arteries (Ruggeri, 2007). Inhibition of this interaction attenuates shear-dependent thrombosis while minimally affecting tail-bleeding time in preclinical models (Koltsova et al., 2014; Prasannan and Scully, 2021). Anfibatide, a GPIbα-binding snake-venom-derived peptide, has completed phase I evaluation in healthy volunteers, showing a dose-dependent prolongation of platelet adhesion without serious bleeding (Lei et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2021). Caplacizumab, a humanized nanobody targeting the A1 domain of vWF, provides clinical proof-of-concept for therapeutic inhibition of GP1b-vWF axis (Peyvandi et al., 2016; Scully et al., 2019). In patients with immune-mediated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (iTTP), clinical trials demonstrated faster platelet count recovery and reduced ischemic complications without marked increase in life-threatening bleeding (Albanell-Fernandez et al., 2023; Volker et al., 2020). However, real-world studies have reported higher rates of clinically relevant non-major bleeding-particularly mucocutaneous and gastrointestinal events-highlighting the need for careful patient selection (Neupane et al., 2024; Volker et al., 2023). Targeting this axis may be particularly valuable in diseases characterized by high-shear thrombosis, including ACS, stroke, and thrombosis associated with mechanical circulatory support devices.

GPIIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβIII): The integrin αIIbβ3 (also known as GPIIb/IIIa) is the most abundant adhesion receptor on the platelet surface, mediating the final step of platelet aggregation. Upon platelet activation by various agonists—such as ADP, thrombin, or collagen—inside-out signaling converts αIIbβ3 from a low-affinity to high-affinity conformation, enabling binding to soluble ligands including fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, and fibronectin (Buitrago et al., 2020; Lefkovits et al., 1995).

Pharmacologic inhibition of the GPIIb/IIIa receptor produces immediate and near-complete suppression of platelet aggregation, making this drug class among the most potent antiplatelet interventions developed (Rosove, 2004; Scarborough et al., 1993; Zavalloniand Rossi, 2004). Intravenous GPIIb/IIIa antagonists—abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban—have demonstrated efficacy in PCI, particularly in patients with high thrombus burden or no-reflow phenomena (Berkowitz, 2000). These agents act by blocking the ligand-binding pocket of αIIbβ3, thereby preventing fibrinogen cross-linking and subsequent platelet aggregation. However, their clinical use has declined due to a high incidence of bleeding and immune-mediated thrombocytopenia, which limit application to bail-out or rescue scenarios rather than routine use.

Contemporary research aims to redefine this pharmacologic class through the development of short-acting, reversible, and subcutaneous formulations intended for prehospital or early ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) care. Molecules such as RUC-4 and zalunfiban provide rapid, transient inhibition of αIIbβ3, enabling early reperfusion therapy while reducing prolonged bleeding risk (Bor et al., 2021; Mattheij et al., 2013). This next-generation approach seeks to retain the potency of classic GPIIb/IIIa blockade but reframe it within a hemostasis-sparing, time-limited therapeutic window, aligning with modern goals of precision and safety in acute arterial thrombosis management.

CLEC-2–podoplanin signaling: CLEC-2 is a platelet hemITAM receptor whose primary physiological role lies not in classical hemostasis, but in vascular–lymphatic separation and lymphatic endothelial integrity. Its endogenous ligand, podoplanin, is minimally expressed on blood vascular endothelium and instead localized to lymphatic endothelium, stromal fibroblasts, and specialized tissue-resident cells. CLEC-2 contributes primarily to lymphatics-associated signaling and tumor-induced platelet activation, not to GPVI- or thrombin-driven physiological hemostasis (Lowe et al., 2012; Suzuki-Inoue, 2019; Suzuki-Inoue et al., 2011).

Pathologically, CLEC-2–podoplanin interactions become prominent in tumor-induced platelet activation and thrombo-inflammation. Many podoplanin-expressing tumors—such as squamous cell carcinoma, glioblastoma, and certain hematologic cancers—activate CLEC-2 to promote platelet–tumor aggregation, metastatic dissemination, and microvascular thrombosis (Suzuki-Inoue et al., 2007).

Because CLEC-2 contributes minimally to physiological hemostasis, its inhibition appears hemostasis-sparing in several preclinical models. Platelet-specific CLEC-2 deficiency produces normal bleeding times yet attenuates tumor-associated platelet activation and inflammatory thrombus formation (Hughes et al., 2010; Meng et al., 2021). Nonetheless, antibody-mediated CLEC-2 depletion has produced variable bleeding effects depending on model and method, indicating the need for translational caution.

Although no clinical CLEC-2–targeted agents exist, this pathway represents a promising non-hemostatic platelet activation mechanism disproportionately engaged in cancer and inflammation. Pharmacologic inhibition of CLEC-2 may therefore offer a hemostasis-preserving approach to mitigating tumor-associated thrombosis and thrombo-inflammation without the bleeding liabilities of conventional antiplatelet therapies.

sec.title: Intracellular signaling axes
sec.p: NADPH oxidase (NOX): Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated by NADPH oxidase (NOX) enzymes act as key secondary messengers downstream of platelet adhesion receptors such as GPVI and GPIb (Violi and Pignatelli, 2014). Among the NOX isoforms, NOX1 and NOX2 are predominant in platelets, catalyzing superoxide (O₂•⁻) formation in response to collagen or shear stress (Walsh et al., 2014). This redox signaling amplifies intracellular Ca²⁺ mobilization, granule secretion, and integrin αIIbβ₃ activation, thereby reinforcing platelet aggregation and thrombus formation.

Pharmacologic inhibition or genetic deletion of NOX isoforms markedly attenuates platelet activation and arterial thrombosis without significantly affecting primary hemostasis (Altenhofer et al., 2015; Chocry and Leloup, 2020). The pan-NOX inhibitor APX-115, developed as an orally bioavailable redox-modulatory compound, was among the earliest next-generation inhibitors shown to potently suppress ROS-dependent platelet activation and FeCl₃-induced thrombosis in preclinical models (Chocry and Leloup, 2020; Jang et al., 2025). Subsequently, setanaxib (GKT137831), a dual NOX1/4 inhibitor, further confirmed these findings by reducing collagen-induced platelet aggregation and arterial thrombosis while preserving hemostasis (Oh et al., 2024). More recently, GSK2795039, a selective NOX2 inhibitor from GlaxoSmithKline, demonstrated robust suppression of ROS production and platelet aggregation ex vivo, validating the key role of NOX2-derived ROS in thrombus amplification (Chocry and Leloup, 2020; Oh et al., 2025). Collectively, these studies support the concept that NOX-derived ROS act as amplifiers rather than initiators of platelet activation. Thus, selective inhibition of NOX1/2 represents a promising hemostasis-sparing antithrombotic strategy with translational potential.

SYK–BTK–PLCγ2 cascade: Signal propagation from ITAM-bearing receptors (GPVI, CLEC-2) is mediated by SYK and its downstream effector BTK, leading to PLCγ2 activation and Ca²⁺ release (Senis et al., 2014). Selective inhibition of SYK or BTK reduces thrombus formation in vivo while leaving primary hemostasis largely intact (Berton et al., 2005; Quek et al., 1998).

SYK inhibitors such as fostamatinib (approved for immune thrombocytopenia) and next-generation compounds (cevidoplenib, lanraplenib) exhibit on-target platelet suppression at low micromolar concentrations (Gonzalez-Lopez et al., 2024; Newland and McDonald, 2020). BTK inhibitors, originally developed for B-cell malignancies, have revealed unexpected antiplatelet effects; however, first-generation covalent inhibitors (ibrutinib) were associated with bleeding due to off-target tyrosine kinase expressed in hepatocellular carcinoma (TEC) inhibition (Bye et al., 2015; Mendez-Ruiz et al., 2023). Second-generation reversible BTK inhibitors (acalabrutinib, pirtobrutinib) show reduced bleeding incidence (Frustaci et al., 2023; Series et al., 2019). Selective, reversible BTK blockade may thus provide a safer means to attenuate platelet signaling.

PI3Kβ and downstream kinases: PI3Kβ integrates signals from both GPCR and ITAM receptors, regulating integrin activation and thrombus stabilization (Garcia et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2009). Mice lacking PI3Kβ display reduced arterial thrombosis with normal bleeding times (Laurent et al., 2015). The isoform-selective inhibitor TGX-221 and its clinical analog AZD6482 demonstrated potent antithrombotic activity in human studies, lowering platelet aggregation without prolonging bleeding (Chen et al., 2019; Nylander et al., 2012). Although development was discontinued for non-efficacy reasons, the concept of isoform-selective PI3Kβ inhibition remains compelling.

Additional intracellular modulators: Other intracellular targets include 12-LOX, involved in oxylipin signaling and integrin activation; its inhibitor ML355 decreases thrombosis without affecting hemostasis (Yeung and Holinstat, 2011; Yeung et al., 2020). PDI participates in platelet aggregation and thrombin generation, and small-molecule PDI inhibitors such as quercetin-3-rutinoside suppress thrombosis in vivo (Flaumenhaft, 2013; Jasuja et al., 2012; Zwicker et al., 2019). These findings suggest that finely tuned inhibition of platelet intracellular enzymes may yield safer antiplatelet profiles.

sec.title: TRANSLATIONAL PERSPECTIVES AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
sec.p: A consistent theme across these mechanistic innovations is the pursuit of selectivity—targeting pathological thrombosis while preserving primary hemostasis. Several translational directions have emerged: (i) Hemostasis-sparing design: Upstream targets such as GPVI, GPIb–vWF, and PI3Kβ regulate thrombus formation only under high-shear or strong stimulation, sparing baseline haemostatic responses. This provides a physiological “selectivity filter” (Rana et al., 2019). (ii) Combination and de-escalation strategies: new agents may complement low-intensity P2Y12 inhibition or short-course DAPT, mitigating ischemic risk without bleeding penalty. The TWILIGHT and STOPDAPT-2 trials have already validated such de-escalation paradigms (Mehran et al., 2019; Watanabe et al., 2019). (iii) Patient stratification and precision therapy: Integration of platelet function testing, genetic polymorphism data, and bleeding risk scores such as PRECISE-DAPT and ARC-HBR allows tailoring of therapy intensity (Kadiyala et al., 2023; Marschall et al., 2024). (iv) Novel biomarkers and imaging: Flow-based microfluidic assays and intravital microscopy are increasingly used to quantify thrombus formation dynamics and evaluate target engagement for emerging agents (Mihalko et al., 2024). (v) Emerging clinical evidence: The ACTIMIS and ACTISAVE phase II trials for glenzocimab have confirmed safety and a trend toward improved ischemic outcomes in stroke (Mazighi et al., 2024; Wichaiyo et al., 2022). Similarly, reversible BTK inhibitors (pirtobrutinib, fenebrutinib) have shown reduced bleeding rates compared with ibrutinib in pooled analyses (Frustaci et al., 2023). (vi) Outstanding challenge: Translating preclinical selectivity into clinical safety remains difficult, as platelet–coagulation cross-talk and off-target kinase inhibition can reintroduce bleeding risk. Large-scale randomized studies are required to validate the “hemostasis-sparing” hypothesis.

In conclusion, the landscape of antiplatelet therapy is shifting from non-selective blockade of amplification pathways toward mechanism-guided, hemostasis-preserving strategies. Targeting adhesion receptors and intracellular signaling kinases holds significant promise for safer thrombosis prevention, bridging the gap between efficacy and safety in cardiovascular and thrombo-inflammatory disease.

caption.p: Potential intracellular signaling targets for novel antiplatelet agents. Upon vascular injury, subendothelial collagen engages GPVI, triggering phosphorylation of the FcRγ chain and activation of SYK, Vav1, BTK, and PLCγ2, which lead to intracellular Ca²⁺ mobilization, granule secretion, and integrin αIIbβ₃ activation. The NOX complex–derived reactive oxygen species (ROS) further amplify platelet activation, whereas cyclic nucleotide signaling through cAMP and cGMP acts as a negative regulatory pathway. Representative compounds targeting these signaling nodes include Revacept and sGPVI–CD133 (GPVI inhibitors), PRT060318, BI1002494, and Entospletinib (SYK inhibitors), Acalabrutinib, Evobrutinib, Tirabrutinib, Remibrutinib, BGB-3111, and Zanubrutinib (BTK inhibitors), Setanaxib, APX-115, VAS2870/VAS3947, and GSK2795039 (NOX inhibitors), Selatogrel, SAR216471, and AZD1283 (P2Y₁₂ antagonists), Riociguat and Iloprost (cyclic nucleotide modulators), Cilostazol, Dipyridamole, and Sildenafil (PDE inhibitors), and Zalunfiban (αIIbβ₃ antagonist). These agents collectively represent emerging strategies to achieve hemostasis-sparing inhibition of platelet activation downstream of collagen and ADP receptor signaling. AC, adenylyl cyclase; Btk, Bruton’s tyrosine kinase; cAMP, cyclic adenosine monophosphate; cGMP, cyclic guanosine monophosphate; GC, guanylyl cyclase; GPVI, glycoprotein VI; LAT, linker for activation of T cells; NOX, NADPH oxidase; PDE, phosphodiesterase; PLCγ2, phospholipase Cγ2; ROS, reactive oxygen species; SYK, spleen tyrosine kinase.

Major receptor pathways mediating platelet activation. Platelet activation is initiated through distinct receptor systems responding to vascular injury and soluble agonists. Collagen exposure triggers platelet adhesion via GPIb–IX–V–vWF interactions under high shear and firm attachment through GPVI and α2β1 integrins. These adhesive events induce intracellular signaling and cytoskeletal reorganization that prime platelets for activation. Simultaneously, soluble agonists—thrombin, ADP, and thromboxane A₂ (TXA₂)—amplify activation through PAR1/PAR4, P2Y₁/P2Y₁₂, and TXA₂ receptors, respectively. Convergent signaling from these receptors leads to granule secretion, activation of integrin αIIbβ₃, and fibrinogen bridging, resulting in stable platelet aggregation and thrombus formation. ADP, adenosine diphosphate; GPVI, glycoprotein VI; GPIb–IX–V, glycoprotein Ib–IX–V complex; PAR, protease-activated receptor; TXA₂, thromboxane A₂; vWF, von Willebrand factor.
